verdict.headline: US strikes on Iranian tankers push oil to a two-month high, but only short rates move
verdict.label: Brent traded above $100 for the first time since July 24, up 2.57% to about $100.44, after US forces destroyed five Iranian tankers; the two-year yield rose two basis points to 4.413% while the ten-year was unchanged at 4.786% and the long end was marginally lower, with equity futures little changed and gold up 1.1% above $4,400
verdict.rationale_short:
Brent traded above $100 a barrel for the first time since July 24, up more than 2.5% to about $100.44, after US Central Command destroyed five Iranian crude tankers on Tuesday in response to two attempted ballistic-missile attacks on a Navy warship in as many days. It was the second US operation against Iranian export assets in four days, after three tankers were disabled near Kharg Island and Jask on September 5. WTI added more than 2% toward $95. From early August's sub-$80 print, that is roughly a $20 move in five weeks.

The US bond market's answer was confined to the short end. The two-year yield rose two basis points to 4.413% shortly after 5:30 AM ET, while the ten-year was unchanged at 4.786% and twenty- and thirty-year yields were marginally lower. Equity futures were little changed — S&P 500 futures up 0.10%, Nasdaq 100 futures 0.22%, Dow futures down 0.02% — gold rose 1.1% to $4,402.41 an ounce and the dollar index eased 0.2% to 98.70. A curve that flattens on an oil shock is pricing a Fed that responds to the shock, not an inflation expectation coming loose. Hike odds for the September 16 decision remain near 59%.

Two things separate this from Tuesday's session. The escalation moved from proxy to direct: Tuesday was priced off Houthi strikes on Saudi facilities, whereas overnight it was US forces striking Iranian export assets themselves, which puts each side's next response in its own hands rather than a client's. And a demand leg arrived underneath the supply story — Chinese crude imports reached 8.93 million barrels a day in August, up 6.2% on July and a second month of recovery from June's decade low. That changes what unwinds on a settlement: a Hormuz transit agreement removes the war premium, not the buying.

The evidence at the long end is genuinely ambiguous, and it should not be over-read in either direction. Treasury's doubled long-end buyback operations take effect today, raising the maximum from $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation across the 10-to-20 and 20-to-30 year sectors through November 4. A mechanical bid arriving at exactly the maturities that declined to move this morning means today's calm cannot yet be separated into judgement about inflation versus purchased demand. Several operations have to run before that distinction is available.

Gold is the one signal that changed sides. It fell 0.84% on Tuesday's escalation, which located the marginal seller in rate expectations rather than in fear; this morning it rose 1.1% back above $4,400 with the dollar lower, the first session this week in which the haven and the barrel moved together.

What would change the picture: WTI is about $0.33 below $95 and the ten-year 3.2 basis points below 4.818%, a level that has now held for a fifth session. WTI through without the ten-year through leaves the front-end-only pricing intact. Both through would say the long end has stopped treating the oil move as something the Fed will absorb. Friday's CPI is August data and cannot contain this week's crude — consensus is 0.3% month over month and 2.9% year over year, core 0.3% and 3.1% — so a hot print would say pass-through was already running before Brent reached $100, which bears on the September 16 decision more than the level of crude does.
verdict.lede_short: Brent traded above $100 for the first time since July 24 after US forces destroyed five Iranian tankers, roughly a $20 move in five weeks. The bond market answered only at the front end — the two-year rose two basis points to 4.413% while the ten-year was unchanged and the long end fell — which prices a Fed response rather than an inflation shock. WTI through $95 alongside the ten-year through 4.818% would change that.

watchlist_mentions.note: WTI added more than 2% toward $95, about $0.33 below the threshold tracked here, while Brent cleared $100 for the first time since July 24. The move is now carrying a demand leg as well as a supply loss: Chinese imports were 8.93 million barrels a day in August, up 6.2%. The EIA weekly petroleum report, the first supply data since the Saudi outages, has moved from today to Thursday at noon because of the September 7 federal closure, so it now lands alongside PPI rather than ahead of it.

The 'Surprise and shine' event begins at 1:00 PM ET, the first under CEO John Ternus, with a foldable iPhone expected to start between $2,099 and $2,299 alongside the iPhone 18 Pro line. A device priced roughly double the current flagship is a test of pricing power rather than of unit demand. The stock closed near $319 after declining 1.17% on Tuesday, without pre-positioning in either direction.

Spot gold rose 1.1% to $4,402.41 an ounce with the dollar index down 0.2% at 98.70, reversing Tuesday's 0.84% decline on an escalation day. It is the first session this week in which the haven bid and crude moved together, and it came with hike odds for September 16 still near 59% — so the change is in the gold bid, not in the rate path.

Traded near $78,912, up about 0.45% and $912 above the $78,000 downside reference, a seventh session below $80,000. It took no meaningful bid from the escalation even as gold rose 1.1%, which continues to separate it from the haven trade rather than from risk appetite.

No company news, but Fortum rose 9.6% to lead the STOXX 600 after signing a long-term power purchase agreement with Google. It is evidence that datacenter power contracting is still being signed at scale while energy prices rise, which is the demand backdrop behind on-site generation.

trade_setups.asset: WTI at $95 against the ten-year at 4.818%
trade_setups.thesis: Brent cleared $100 for the first time since July 24 and WTI added more than 2% toward $95, while the US curve repriced only at the front end — the two-year up two basis points to 4.413%, the ten-year unchanged at 4.786%, the long end marginally lower. Either the bond market has judged that the Fed will absorb the oil move, or the long end has not yet repriced it; at this distance from the level the two are indistinguishable. 4.818% has held for a fifth session.
trade_setups.entry: $95 on WTI, about $0.33 away, and 4.818% on the ten-year, 3.2 basis points away. WTI through without the ten-year through keeps the front-end-only pricing intact; both through says the long end has stopped treating this as a Fed problem.
trade_setups.invalidation: The Iran-Oman Hormuz transit agreement, described as in its final stages, would take the war premium out of crude — though not the Chinese buying underneath it. Crude retreating while the two-year holds 4.4% would separate the supply story from the policy story rather than resolve either.
trade_setups.horizon: This week, into the September 16 FOMC

trade_setups.asset: The long end while Treasury buybacks double
trade_setups.thesis: Treasury's long-end operations rise from a $2 billion to an at-least-$4 billion maximum today and run through November 4, covering the 10-to-20 and 20-to-30 year sectors — exactly the maturities that were marginally lower on a morning crude broke $100. The thirty-year sits near 5.251%, about five basis points under 5.30%, a level it has traded through twice without a close above it. A mechanical bid and a considered judgement about inflation look identical in a single session's price.
trade_setups.entry: 5.30% on the thirty-year and 4.818% on the ten-year are the levels; the number of buyback operations run is the variable that separates the two explanations.
trade_setups.invalidation: The long end selling off through those levels while the operations are live would say supply dynamics are overwhelming $4 billion per operation. Holding through Thursday's PPI, which is a genuine inflation input rather than a flow, would be the first evidence the calm is judgement.
trade_setups.horizon: Through November 4, tested first on Thursday

trade_setups.asset: August CPI as a read on pass-through that predates $100 crude
trade_setups.thesis: Friday's CPI covers August and therefore cannot contain this week's move in crude. Consensus is 0.3% month over month and 2.9% year over year, with core at 0.3% and 3.1%; July already carried gasoline up 24.6% and fuel oil 39.1%. PPI lands Thursday first, and the FOMC is in blackout through September 17, so no official can frame either print. Hike odds for September 16 sit near 59%.
trade_setups.entry: 0.3% month over month on core is the consensus line. The September print, released in October, is the first that can carry $100 Brent.
trade_setups.invalidation: A CPI at or below consensus would say the pass-through visible in producer prices has not reached the consumer even at July's energy levels, which would make the front-end repricing look early rather than prescient.
trade_setups.horizon: Thursday and Friday, into the September 16 decision
